title: Raga Maru
hook: the raga of courage, traditionally sung before battle

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Mali Gaura, and your line was sweet and short. Which ordinary thing got your sentence of thanks? Day one thousand one hundred six.

This week the ragas kept changing color. Ramkali, calm and deep. Nat Narain, lively. Mali Gaura, short and sweet, with Namdev blessing the wool. Now the mood turns. The next section of the Guru Granth Sahib is Raga Maru, and tradition says it was sung before battle, when people needed their nerve. After a week of calm, lively and sweet, the Granth turns to a hard mood to sing about: being afraid, and going anyway. Today, Raga Maru.

Maru is a long section, and it holds hymns that look hard things in the face: death, loss, the shortness of a life. Tradition remembers it as a raga for the eve of battle. Tomorrow we'll open one of its hymns. Today, the color itself: courage. And to hear what courage means in this tradition, go back to the very first page of the Granth. The Mul Mantar, the root statement, names the One with a short list. Among its words are nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hate. They sit side by side. That pairing matters. The courage the Granth honors isn't the courage of someone who's angry enough to stop being scared. It's fearlessness with no hatred in it. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, puts it in one line near the end of the Granth. Given here in plain English, not word for word: the wise one frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves count. Someone who fears no one but frightens everyone isn't the picture. Neither is someone who frightens no one only because they're too scared to stand up. Maru holds both halves. Tradition ties it to the eve of battle, and at the same time its hymns keep pointing past the battlefield, to the fear inside a person, of loss, of being judged, of dying, and to the Name as the ground to stand on. So the raga of battle is also a raga of steadiness. That's today's line: courage.
screen: `A RAGA FOR THE EVE OF BATTLE.` · `NIRBHAU AND NIRVAIR, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `THE FEAR INSIDE, THE GROUND TO STAND ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand your ground, sitting down. Plant your feet flat on the floor and feel their weight. Let your back be tall. Now bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because it scares you a little: a phone call, a hard conversation, an honest no. Don't solve it. Just look at it from where you sit, feet planted. Breathe in, and feel the ground under you. Breathe out, and let go of any blame you've attached to it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. If you don't, simply keep your feet planted and your breath steady. Later today, listen to one Maru shabad. The bell holds the time.
Raga Maru. The raga tradition remembers being sung before battle, whose courage, in the Granth's terms, is without fear and without hate. Today's word.
Your line: courage. Today, do the small, slightly scary thing from your sit, and do it without making anyone else afraid. Day one thousand one hundred six. A week done.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Maru section are sung in Raga Maru in kirtan. Sikhs recite the Mul Mantar, with its words nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of daily prayer, and it stands at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib.

what it means: Maru, the raga of courage, whose hymns point to the fear inside and the Name as ground to stand on.
what a scholar hears: courage in the Granth is defined from its first page, nirbhau beside nirvair, and echoed in Guru Tegh Bahadur's frighten no one, fear no one.
